analysis.one_liner: Promises trade deals a straight up-or-down vote in Congress with no amendments, and lets the President negotiate them.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed it 62-38, the House agreed 219-211, and the President signed it into law on June 29, 2015, giving the White House about six years of expedited trade-deal authority.
analysis.plain_summary: This is the 2015 "fast track" trade bill (trade promotion authority). It sets a list of negotiating objectives for U.S. trade agreements and, in exchange, guarantees that any deal the President finishes gets special expedited treatment in Congress: limited debate, no amendments allowed, and a single up-or-down vote in each chamber, with the authority running through mid-2018 and extendable to 2021. In practice, it was written to let the White House finish and win approval of deals like the Trans-Pacific Partnership, whose provisions on intellectual property, cross-border data flows, and protections for investors abroad matter most to large exporters, drug makers, and technology and entertainment companies. The President must consult Congress and meet the objectives, but Congress's role once a deal arrives is take-it-or-leave-it.
analysis.who_benefits: The President, who gains negotiating leverage because trading partners know Congress cannot rewrite the finished deal. Large exporters — agribusiness, multinational manufacturers, pharmaceutical companies, and technology and entertainment firms — benefit because the negotiating objectives are built around their priorities: strong intellectual property rules similar to U.S. law, free cross-border data flows, protections and dispute mechanisms for investors abroad, and opening foreign markets to U.S. goods and services. Congressional leaders also benefit, because fast-track rules concentrate control over trade votes in leadership and keep amendments off the floor.

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes the President to negotiate agreements reducing tariffs and other trade barriers before July 1, 2018 — or 2021 if the authority is extended — and to proclaim the necessary duty changes himself.

Applies the "trade authorities procedures" of the Trade Act of 1974 to implementing bills, meaning a finished deal comes to the floor under limited debate with no amendments and an up-or-down vote — the guarantee trading partners need before they make their own concessions.

Directs U.S. negotiators to seek intellectual property protection comparable to U.S. law, to prevent restrictions on cross-border data flows and data storage requirements, and to preserve investor protections and dispute-resolution mechanisms, while expressing support for the Doha Declaration on access to medicines.

Specially covers agreements with Trans-Pacific Partnership and European Union countries begun before enactment, along with WTO agreements — putting the biggest deals then in negotiation squarely under its expedited procedures.

analysis.who_pays: Workers and communities in import-sensitive industries — manufacturing, textiles and apparel, some agriculture — carry the risk of job and production losses from the deals this authority was designed to finish, with protection limited to longer phase-in periods and consultations for sensitive products. Congress itself cedes power: once a qualifying deal arrives, members cannot offer amendments and debate is capped. The public also gives up leverage, because the USTR is required to publish summaries of negotiating objectives, not the full text of the agreement before it is signed.

drawbacks.text: Once an agreement qualifies, members of Congress cannot offer amendments and debate is limited, so 535 lawmakers vote yes or no on hundreds of pages of negotiated text with no ability to fix specific problems — even for provisions that change U.S. law.

The labor and environment provisions are negotiating objectives and consultation requirements, not new domestic protections; the text expressly lets a trading partner's "bona fide" choices about how to allocate enforcement resources count as compliance.

The transparency additions are modest: a Chief Transparency Officer inside the USTR, summaries of objectives posted before negotiations start, and advisory access for congressional advisers to classified documents — not a requirement that the full negotiating text be public before an agreement is signed.

The bill's stated tariff-cutting authority is broad, while protections for import-sensitive products consist mainly of staging schedules, longer adjustment periods, and required consultations rather than veto points.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters' case is real: without a guarantee of an up-or-down vote, trading partners will not put their best offers on the table, and the bill does add consultation requirements, congressional advisory groups, a transparency officer, and labor, environment, and anti-bribery negotiating objectives. The cost side is structural: the binding part of the bill is the procedure, not the objectives. Objectives can be missed without penalty, while the no-amendment, limited-debate vote is guaranteed. That design hands the most consequential decisions — over intellectual property, investor protections, and regulatory rules that reach into domestic law — to negotiators and the industries that advise them, and leaves members of Congress a binary choice on a finished package. An honest supporter would concede the enforcement teeth for labor and environment are soft compared with the procedural teeth for completing the deal.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it with an amendment 62-38 in late May 2015, the House agreed to the Senate version 219-211 on June 12, 2015, and the President signed it into law on June 29, 2015 as Public Law 114-26.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Ryan (R-WI) introduced the bill on April 17, 2015, with three cosponsors (Reps. Sessions, Tiberi, and Cuellar), and it was referred to the Ways and Means, Rules, and Budget Committees.
The Ways and Means Committee ordered it reported amended on April 23 and reported it on May 1, 2015 (H. Rept. 114-100, Part I), and it was placed on the Union Calendar (No. 69).
The Senate passed the bill with an amendment by a 62-38 vote in May 2015, and the House agreed to the Senate amendment by a 219-211 recorded vote on June 12, 2015.

The bill requires Congress to consult with the executive branch before and during negotiations and creates congressional advisory groups on negotiations and a Chief Transparency Officer within the USTR.
The President signed it on June 29, 2015, and it became Public Law 114-26, the Bipartisan Congressional Trade Priorities and Accountability Act of 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Presidency and the export- and IP-heavy industries whose priorities were written into the negotiating objectives — they got a six-year guarantee that finished deals would get clean up-or-down votes. Congress traded its power to amend trade deals for consultation rights. Notably, the flagship deal this authority was built for, the Trans-Pacific Partnership, was later signed but never brought to a vote, so the expedited authority went largely unused for the deal it was created to pass.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The White House and export-focused industries

for.name: Paul Ryan
for.role: Chairman, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, managed it through committee markup, and steered it to House passage, 219-211.

for.name: Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Personally pressed members of his own party to support the bill and signed it into law on June 29, 2015.

for.name: 48 of 54 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage, forming the bulk of the 62-38 majority.

for.name: 14 of 44 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage, providing the bipartisan margin in the Senate.

for.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and allied business groups
for.what_they_did: Ran a sustained campaign for fast-track authority as essential to completing the Pacific trade deal.

against.name: Majority of House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, supplying most of the 211 no votes in the 219-211 House tally.

against.name: Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the expedited process and did not whip her members for the bill, leaving most of the caucus free to vote no.

against.name: AFL-CIO and allied labor unions
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against fast track, arguing the deals it enabled would cost manufacturing jobs and give corporations channels to challenge domestic rules.

against.name: Senate Democrats in opposition
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage in the 62-38 Senate tally.

sides.party_line_note: The bill passed on heavily partisan votes — 62-38 in the Senate and 219-211 in the House — with Republicans supplying the bulk of the yes votes, while most Democrats opposed it; a sizable minority crossed over on each side, with 14 Senate Democrats and roughly 75 House Republicans voting against their party's majority position.

industries.note: The bill directs negotiators to seek IP protections similar to U.S. law and strong enforcement abroad, the core of drug-industry demands in trade deals. Longer and stronger exclusivity in trading partners slows cheaper generics, which shows up for consumers as higher drug prices over time, even though the text also pledges respect for the Doha Declaration on access to medicines.

The bill instructs negotiators to preserve investor protections and investor-state dispute mechanisms, with some added transparency and frivolous-claim deterrence. These channels let foreign companies bring arbitration claims against governments over regulation, a power ordinary citizens and domestic businesses do not have.

industries.industry: Technology, entertainment, and other IP-reliant firms
industries.note: The bill directs negotiators to block restrictions on cross-border data flows and local data storage and to extend the WTO moratorium on internet duties, priorities of digital-economy firms. Open data flows benefit internet users too, while stronger copyright and enforcement objectives raise costs for consumers.

The bill directs negotiators to open foreign markets and cut foreign tariffs and subsidies, the main asks of farm and manufacturing exporters. Consumers may see lower prices, but import-sensitive producers and their workers bear the adjustment risk.

The bill requires consultations before tariff cuts on sensitive farm products and textiles and preserves limits on how far tariffs on those products can fall without new legislation. These are partial shields, not protection — the bill's overall thrust is market opening.

Fast track makes it far harder for the workers' allies in Congress to amend trade deals to strengthen labor and environment terms, since finished agreements come to the floor with no amendments allowed.
